DILG DACONO PIUP'NAS Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilg.qpv.ph OILG OPINION NO. 3q MAR 0 3 2025 Concerned Citizen justaconcernedcitizenofph@gmail.com To whom it may concern: This has reference to your email dated January 13, 2025, requesting this Department to comment on Section 141 , Article XXV of Ordinance No. 08-s-2016, enacted by the City of Dasmarifias which grants the local traffic enforcement officer authority to confiscate driver's license for violating local traffic rules and regulation, thus the ordinance reads — "Section 141. PROCEDURES IN THE ISSUANCE OF TRAFFIC CITATION TICKET Any person violating any provision of this Ordinance shall be issued a Traffic Citation Ticket (TCT). In case of violation of the Traffic Management Code, a duly deputized traffic enforcement officer shall confiscate the drivers license, and the issued receipt shall serve as Temporary Driver's License for five (5) days from the date of issuance. TCT issued by other local government units shall be honored or respected by the apprehending traffic enforcer. " You believe this ordinance appears to be in direct conflict with national law, specifically the provisions under the Land Transportation and Traffic Codel. Consequently, such ordinance not only diminishes the authority of the national government but, also, establishes a perilous precedent for other local government units to emulate, which could jeopardize the constitutional framework that delineates the balance of powers between national and local authorities. Presently, your request is for this Department to conduct a review of the ordinance in question, and if possible, implement preventive measures for its enforcement. Furthermore, you seek clarification regarding the Department's responsibilities towards Local Government Units (LGUs), particularly concerning the policy measures implemented; the enforcement mechanisms utilized by DILG to ensure that LGUs develop their regulations in alignment with national policies; and, lastly, the coordination strategies employed by DILG with other national agencies. We discuss. 1 Republic Act NO. 4136. "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline NO.: 8876-34-54

At the outset, DILG plays a critical role in maintaining good governance and ensuring that LGUs operate within the legal framework set by the national laws. Local ordinances, while essential for addressing community-specific concerns, must not contradict legal statutes. In Tatel vs. Municipality of Virac, et. al.2 the Supreme Court stated that, it is a settled principle of law that municipal corporations are agencies of the State for the promotion and maintonanco or local self-government and as such are endowed with the police powots in ordor to offoctivoly accomplish and carry out the declared objects of their creation. Its authority emanates from the general welfare clause under the Administrative Code, which roads: "The municipal council shall enact such ordinances and make such tegulations, not repugnant to law, as may be necessary to carry into effect and discharge the powers and duties conferred upon it by law and such as shall seem necessary and proper to provide for the health and safety, promote the prosperity, improve the morals, peace, good order, comfort and convenience of the municipality and the inhabitants thereof, and for the protection of property therein. " For an ordinance to be valid, it must not only be within the corporate powers of the municipality to enact but must also be passed according to the procedure prescribed by law, and must be in consonance with certain well established and basic principles of a substantive nature. These principles require that a municipal ordinance (1) must not contravene the Constitution or any statute (2) must not be unfair or oppressive (3) must not be partial or discriminatory (4) must not prohibit but may regulate trade (5) must be general and consistent with public policy, and (6) must not be unreasonable. Hence, as long as the subject ordinance adheres to the aforementioned requirements, it remains valid, and this Department lacks the authority to invalidate it. Additionally, this Department wishes to reiterate that while it exercises the power of general supervision over LGUs and its officials, it is beyond its authority to review, nullify or declare local ordinances as invalid. This is based on the presumption of validity accorded to local legislative enactments. The power to review ordinances lies with the reviewing Sanggunian in accordance with Sec. 56 of the Local Government Code as well as the judiciary if the ordinances are challenged for being unconstitutional or illegal. You assert that the authority to confiscate licenses resides with the Land Transportation Office (LTO) in accordance with Republic Act No. 4136. We beg to disagree. While it may be true that the Land Transportation Office (L TO) is the primary government agency in the Philippines responsible for enforcing traffic laws. Nonetheless, the law also gives LTO the authority to deputize other entities, including Local Government Units (LGUs), to assist in enforcing traffic laws and regulations. Section 29 of Republic Act No. 4136 states that — Section 29. Confiscation of driver's licenses. - Law enforcement and peace officers duly designated by the Commissioner shall, in apprehending any driver for violations of this Act or of any regulations issued pursuant thereto, or of local traffic rules and G.R. NO. 40243, March 11, 1992. Page 2 of 3

regulations, confiscate the license of the driver concerned and issue a receipt prescribed and issued by tho Commission This deputization allows LGUs to perform certain functions, and as clearly stated therein peace officers including local traffic enforcers have the authority to confiscate driver's license and issue the necessary receipt, when local traffic rules are violated. As to your query on the policy measures and enforcement mechanism being implemented, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) provides various policies, advisories, and guidelines to LGUs to ensure that their ordinances align with national policies. These may come in the form of a memorandum circular, legal opinions and other administrative issuances. By providing these to LGUs it gives them a clear policy direction and a reference when drafting ordinances. We invite you to visit our website at https://dilg.gov.ph/ for your reference. Finally, this opinion is based solely on the facts and representations narrated from the letter and our appreciation of the same. Further, this opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have assisted you on this matter. Very truly yours, BY AUTHORITY OF TY-4E SECRETARY: Undersecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs OUSELLA.'RPB,'LLLS-LRALLD/rnag Page 3 of 3
